fatal_errors: The proposed grain-boundary segregation and brittle-precipitation mechanism reproduces the conventional-alloy expectation rather than the target phase-boundary and ordering mechanism.
The initial material is incorrectly treated as a homogeneous single-phase HEA; the target is an as-cast FCC+B2 eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy.
The intervention is changed from isothermal aging across an intermediate-temperature window to high-temperature cyclic loading, introducing an unsupported requirement for applied cyclic stress.
The hypothesis misses enhanced L12 ordering, elevated antiphase-boundary energy, planar slip, jagged FCC/B2 phase boundaries, and crack initiation at phase-boundary tips.
It predicts only toughness degradation rather than the observed non-monotonic ductile-brittle-ductile transition, with minimum ductility near 600 degrees C and recovery near 750 degrees C.
No supporting prior evidence is provided.
explanation: The hypothesis offers a testable factorial comparison and appropriate tools such as APT, TEM, and fracture testing, so its experimental design has some discriminating value. However, it reconstructs neither the material nor the causal mechanism of the target. Temperature is the only limited overlap: approximately 700 degrees C lies within the relevant aging range, but the target response depends on aging-temperature-dependent L12 ordering and FCC/B2 phase-boundary evolution, not stress-assisted grain-boundary precipitation during cyclic loading. The proposed controls also cannot reveal the decisive ductile-brittle-ductile temperature dependence. A target-aligned falsification test would age specimens below 550 degrees C, near 600 degrees C, and near 750 degrees C without cyclic loading, then correlate ductility with L12 order, jagged phase-boundary density, dislocation pile-ups, and crack initiation sites while excluding impurity segregation.
